views.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Keep the dispute on a legal and diplomatic track. Continue WTO compensation consultations on the Section 201 solar and washer safeguards, and use the Liu He channel to probe U.S. intent on Section 301 and Section 232 without offering structural IP or industrial-policy concessions. Do not launch a tariff retaliation package yet: the only U.S. measures actually in force are narrow safeguards, 232 duties are still a presidential decision due in April, and 301 findings have not been issued. Prepare a calibrated retaliation list in reserve if Washington converts the Commerce 232 options or a 301 determination into broad China-specific tariffs.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is real but still prospective, not existential. The August 2017 Section 301 initiation targets the core of China’s technology-transfer and industrial-upgrade model, MOFCOM already rejected U.S. consultations as “irresponsible” and “not objective,” and the November 2017 Beijing summit produced commercial MOUs with no IP concessions—so the structural fight is unresolved. The January 22, 2018 Section 201 tariffs (solar starting at 30%, washers up to 50%) are the first live U.S. tariff action and hit Chinese suppliers; MOFCOM called them an “abuse of trade remedy measures.” Commerce’s February 16 Section 232 reports add a further downside: options include a 24% global steel tariff or at least 53% on a 12-country list that includes China, and 7.7% global or 23.6% China-focused aluminum duties, with a presidential deadline in April. That mix warrants a positive threat reading. It does not warrant a high or existential score: Chinese industrial production is still running ~7.2% YoY, seasonally adjusted merchandise exports jumped in February, reserves remain ~$3.15tn, the discount rate is unchanged at 2.9%, and CNY has strengthened (about 6.33 per dollar vs ~6.53 in early September)—so the dispute is not yet biting the real economy, FX, or financial stability. Action should therefore stay near zero. China has already chosen the right first move—WTO filings in early February seeking Article 8.1 compensation talks, alongside South Korea and Taiwan—and premature tariff retaliation would undercut that multilateral positioning while giving Washington a pretext to accelerate 301/232. Concessionary purchases or a structural rollback would also be mistimed: talks are not advanced and the U.S. has made no matching offer. Negotiate without new commitments; hold fire on tariffs until a broader U.S. action actually lands.
key_factors: Section 301 IP/tech-transfer investigation is open but findings and remedies are not yet issued
Section 201 solar and washer safeguards are the only live U.S. tariffs and are being contested at the WTO
Section 232 steel/aluminum recommendations (Feb 16) raise the risk of broader duties, including China-specific options, but Trump has not decided
China’s macro picture is still healthy: IP growth, strong exports, stable reserves, firmer CNY — no current export-hub or FX stress
Diplomatic opening via Liu He and WTO Article 8.1 talks allows engagement without structural concessions

sources_cited.excerpt: Trump signs memorandum directing USTR to investigate China's IP and technology-transfer practices under Section 301. USTR investigation initiated.
Trump visits Beijing; large package of commercial deals announced (many MOUs). No substantive concessions on structural IP / tech-transfer issues.
Trump approves Section 201 safeguard tariffs on solar panels and washing machines (China among suppliers hit). First major tariff action of the administration.
China industrial production index 107.2 as of 2018-02-01 (~7.2% YoY); change +1.0 over the window — no visible production hit from the dispute.
China SA merchandise exports 253.3bn USD in Feb 2018, up sharply over the lookback — export economy not yet compressed.
China total reserves ex-gold ~3.15tn USD in Feb 2018, slightly higher over the window — no reserve-drain signal.
CNY strengthened to 6.328 per USD on 2018-02-28 from ~6.53 in early September — FX pressure is not the current problem.
China accused Trump of jeopardizing the multilateral trading system. MOFCOM: the U.S. “again abused its trade remedy measures” and expressed “strong dissatisfaction.”
In early February 2018 China demanded WTO talks on compensation for the solar and washer safeguards, asserting Article 8.1 rights and alleging WTO-inconsistency.
Feb 16, 2018: Commerce recommended a 24% global steel tariff or ≥53% on 12 countries including China, and 7.7% global or 23.5% China-focused aluminum tariffs; Trump has 90 days to decide.
USTR must determine by August 2018 whether China’s APPs are actionable under Section 301; Chinese industry groups at the hearing denied legal tech-transfer mandates.
White House said Liu He would meet U.S. counterparts the week of 28 Feb; MOFCOM separately protested U.S. aluminum-foil dumping duties as WTO-inconsistent.
